Section 01 · Overview

Shark is earning less on more revenue. The cause is concentrated, measurable and largely reversible within two quarters

In this illustration, revenue grew 5.6% to $35.2m in the twelve months to August 2026 while variable contribution fell 8% to $9.4m. Three things explain most of it: an always-on discount that gives back the price increase, marketing that costs a third more per installed job, and two markets that do not yet earn their spend. A three-week diagnostic would confirm each on Shark's own records and hand the board a ranked set of decisions.

The read

Margin is the binding problem, then volume. On illustrative figures calibrated to what management has shared, revenue rose 5.6% to $35.2m while variable contribution fell 8% to $9.4m. The price increase worked; the always-on 15% offer gave it back, marketing now costs a third more per installed job, and two new markets spend ahead of their conversion. Jacksonville and Central Florida remain strong. Six levers are worth $4.8m–7.9m a year; the diagnostic would size each on Shark's own records in fifteen working days.

The question management asked, margin or volume, has a short answer: margin first, then volume

Four numbers carry the story. The fourth is the size of the prize the diagnostic would validate.

Six levers · validated in diagnostic

Five findings explain the year, and each comes with the test that would confirm it

The bridge below is in dollars; tab 03 shows the same bridge in margin points. Eight operating measures moved against the business at the same time, which is why no single fix has shown up in the results.

Two markets earn 92% of contribution, and the cheapest leads are not the cheapest jobs

The issue is concentrated by market and by channel. That concentration is what makes it tractable: most of the business is working.

Four commercial changes in nine months overlapped, which is why tests to date could not separate their effects

Price, promotion, TV and two new markets all moved within the same window, against a seasonal business, while lead volume grew faster than jobs. That is a measurement problem as much as a commercial one.

Six levers are worth $4.8m to $7.9m of annual contribution; the diagnostic would size each on Shark's records in three weeks

The ranges are wide on purpose. They narrow once the job-level join is built, and the diagnostic only books a lever once its test has been designed and read.

Caution

The promotion is costing about $0.5m of contribution a month at the current run-rate. Of all the decisions in this demo, it is the one where waiting carries the clearest cost.

Note

Jacksonville and Central Florida, the review base and the crew bench are real strengths. Nothing in this demo argues for less ambition; it argues for spending where the evidence says it returns.

Section 03 · Margin or volume

It is both, in sequence: contribution has fallen 8% on 5.6% more revenue, and a volume problem sits underneath it

Revenue rose to $35.2m in the twelve months to August 2026, but variable contribution fell from $10.2m to $9.4m and its margin from 30.6% to 26.7%. Flat company volume hides a 7.3% fall in the three established markets, filled by two new markets that do not yet earn their marketing. The diagnostic would confirm each step of this bridge at job level before any lever is pulled.

The read

Both, in sequence. Contribution fell $0.8m on $1.9m more revenue: price added about seven points of margin, the promotion and free removal took back six, marketing intensity three. Underneath, established markets installed 7.3% fewer jobs and every funnel stage converted worse than last year. Fix the margin first because it is faster and larger; recover volume through conversion rather than discount.

Revenue is up and contribution is down: the business is selling the same number of jobs at a higher cost to win them

Four numbers frame the question. Price carried revenue; volume, marketing intensity and the promotion took contribution back.

The price increase added seven points of margin; the promotion and marketing intensity took back nine

The bridge isolates each driver in percentage points of revenue. Price and promotion are close to equal and opposite; marketing intensity and new-market mix explain the rest.

Flat company volume is two new markets filling a 460-job hole in the three established ones

Jacksonville, Central Florida and Tampa installed 7.3% fewer jobs than last year. Treasure Coast and Fort Myers added 498 net jobs at low or negative contribution, so the mix moved against margin as well.

The average job now earns $1,445 of contribution, $128 less than last year on a $257 higher ticket

Per job, the price increase was absorbed by marketing ($201 more per job) and by higher delivery cost as the mix moved toward longer-drive and new markets.

Caution

At the May–August run-rate the promotion costs about $0.5m of contribution a month and returns about $0.03m through extra jobs. Left in place for twelve months it would take VCM toward 20% of revenue.

Note

Restoring last year's funnel and replacing the always-on discount would recover most of the gap within two quarters

The board question is not whether to grow or to protect margin; it is which levers recover contribution without giving up volume. The scenarios and sensitivities below are illustrative and are the first thing the diagnostic would re-cut on actual data.

Section 04 · Marketing spend

The extra $1.33m went to new markets, Meta and a TV test; about $0.75m–$1.1m now sits in pools least likely to be adding jobs

Marketing rose 33% to $5.33m in the twelve months to August 2026 and installed jobs rose by 38. Most of the increase funded two new hubs and the TV test; in the established markets spend was close to flat while cost per job still rose. The demo data points to five pools where dollars are least likely to be incremental, and a reallocation worth $0.6m–$1.0m of contribution that the diagnostic would confirm on job-level data before any budget moves.

The read

The overspend is real but specific. Marketing rose $1.33m to 15.1% of revenue for 38 more installed jobs. The dollars least likely to be incremental sit in four pools — aggregator leads that rarely install, Meta spend above about $35k a week, ads landing more than an hour from a hub, and new-market budgets set ahead of conversion — worth $0.75m–1.1m. Moving about $1.0m of it is worth $0.6m–1.0m of contribution.

Spend rose $1.33m to $5.33m: by channel, Meta and the TV test explain two-thirds; by market, the two new hubs and TV explain all of it

Management's sense that the business is overspending is consistent with the ratios: marketing rose from 12.0% to 15.1% of revenue and from $617 to $818 per installed job. The question is which dollars, which the rest of this tab narrows down.

Spend follows the map less closely than the crews do. Out-of-area leads rarely install, and the markets that need demand most are the ones where each dollar buys the least contribution.

The TV test bought incremental jobs at about $2,050 each: inside the $2,260 break-even, 2.5 times the blended cost, so pulling back is defensible

The $430k flight in Tampa Bay and Orlando from February to May lifted branded search and leads against the control markets. On the read available, it roughly paid for itself and no more. Tab 05 sets out why the design cannot separate TV from season, and how the diagnostic would re-read it.

Note

None of these moves requires a smaller marketing ambition. They move about a fifth of the budget toward demand the crews can serve and that converts, and each would be staged behind a holdout read rather than switched off at once.

Section 05 · Attribution & testing

The current model cannot say whether Meta is under- or over-credited; the diagnostic can, first as a bounded range and then as a measured result

Four systems report Meta's contribution at anywhere from 12,600 leads to 1,372 installed jobs, and the demo data is consistent both with Meta creating demand that other channels collect and with Meta reaching people already in market. Five A/B tests were run in good faith; none had the sample to reach a decision. Joining source to cash at job level and running geo holdouts would settle the Meta question within about ten weeks.

The read

The current measurement cannot say whether Meta is under- or over-credited, and none of the five tests to date could have reached a decision. The pattern fits Meta starting searches that rivals finish: branded search lifts a week after Meta spend and Meta-sourced buyers more often hold competing quotes. A job-level join, offline conversion import and geographic holdouts would let the board read Meta, TV and the promotion on installed jobs within one quarter.

Four systems give four answers for Meta, from 12,600 leads to 1,372 jobs, and none of them measures what Meta causes

The business runs on last-click attribution with manual reconciliation, which is common for an installer of this size. It answers cost per lead; it cannot answer cost per incremental job.

Weeks with more Meta spend lift branded search a week later, and Meta-sourced buyers more often hold a competing quote: Meta may be starting searches that others finish

The halo question is whether Meta ads prompt viewers to research and then collect several quotes. Three pieces of demo evidence point that way; none of them proves it, and they are equally consistent with Meta partly reaching people already in market.

Caution

The lag correlation and the survey show association, not cause. At the low end Meta costs more per job than a job contributes; at the high end it is the cheapest paid channel after LSA, so the budget decision should wait for the holdout read.

One lead in eight now has no usable source, and GA4 cannot see which web visits become installed jobs

The gaps are in the joins, not the tools: Builder Prime, GA4, Meta and Google each hold part of the journey, and nothing connects a click or a call to the cash from the job.

Five A/B tests were run and none could reach a decision: the largest had 28% of the sample it needed, and the TV test could not separate TV from season

The habit of testing is in place, which many businesses of this size lack. The tests were short, measured on early-funnel metrics, or ran alongside the promotion; at Shark's traffic, job-level questions need geo or time-based designs rather than page splits.

Three changes would let the board read Meta, TV and the promotion on installed jobs: a job-level join, offline conversion import and geo holdouts

The diagnostic would build the join in week one, switch on the imports in weeks two and three, and hand over pre-registered holdout designs at the week-three readout. The Meta answer arrives as a bounded range at the readout and as a measured result about eight weeks later.

Note

Nothing here requires replacing Builder Prime or GA4. The work is joins, tags and test discipline, and it leaves management with a model it runs without outside help.

Section 06 · Market maturity

Two hubs earn 92% of contribution; Tampa has held at 10% for eight quarters because two-fifths of its jobs sit beyond an economic drive

Jacksonville and Central Florida matured quickly and remain strong businesses. Tampa reached 10% variable contribution at month 15 and has not moved since, and the two new markets are earlier on a slower curve. The demo data points to service radius rather than competition as the binding constraint in Tampa, and to spend pacing rather than exit in the new markets; the diagnostic would confirm both at job and ZIP level.

The read

Two hubs earn 92% of contribution. Tampa has held near 10% for eight quarters because two-fifths of its jobs sit beyond an economic drive: jobs within 30 minutes earn about 21%, those beyond about 3%. A tighter radius with inward backfill is worth $0.4m–0.6m a year. Neither new market yet meets the proposed gates; pacing spend to the gates protects $0.2m–0.4m without closing either.

Jacksonville and Central Florida earn 92% of contribution on 70% of revenue; Tampa and the two new markets earn 7% on 30%

The hub P&L separates two kinds of gap. Tampa's is in delivery cost, 55.5% of revenue against 40% in Jacksonville. Treasure Coast's and Fort Myers' is in marketing, 30% and 42% of revenue.

Jacksonville and Central Florida crossed 20% within ten months of opening; Tampa reached 10% at month 15 and has held there for eight quarters

Plotted by quarter since opening rather than by calendar, the two mature hubs follow the same path. Tampa flattened at about half their level in its sixth quarter; Treasure Coast is below Tampa's curve at the same age, and the May promotion pushed its fifth quarter negative.

Tampa's margin is set by distance: jobs within 30 minutes of the hub earn 21%, the 59% beyond earn about 3%

Tampa's hub is in Thonotosassa, east of the city, and its service radius extends about 75 miles. The radius was widened in the third quarter of 2025; contribution did not move and jobs fell 11%. The near-hub business looks like Central Florida; the far business carries the callbacks, cancellations and lower close rates.

Caution

Competitor counts come from public location pages and say nothing about capacity or pricing. The diagnostic would map competing-quote presence (A-19) and close rate by ZIP, which is what separates a radius effect from a competition effect.

A 60-minute radius with inward backfill would take Tampa to about 18% VCM and add $0.4m to $0.6m a year

Tampa's crews are as busy as Jacksonville's but spend nearly twice as long on the road. The new markets' crews have the opposite problem: they are short of booked work. Tightening Tampa's radius trades about a fifth of its jobs for a higher-margin, denser book.

Neither new market meets the proposed gates yet; pacing spend to gates would protect $0.2m to $0.4m a year without closing either

Treasure Coast and Fort Myers are young, and new hubs lose money at first. The question for the board is how much marketing and crew capacity each should receive before it has shown the pattern Jacksonville and Central Florida showed by month ten. Explicit gates turn that into a schedule rather than a judgement call each quarter.

Note

The gates are a proposal for the board to calibrate, not a verdict on either market. Treasure Coast was meeting G1 before the promotion, and Fort Myers is at an age when every Shark hub has been negative.

Section 07 · Price & promotion

The price increase paid for itself; the always-on 15% offer has returned about $0.1m of contribution for $2.1m since May

The January increase lifted net ticket 14.6% and cost a modest share of volume, concentrated in garage jobs. The always-on offer that followed was a reasonable response to slowing volume going into the season, but at a 30% margin it needed volume to roughly double and it has added about 6%. The diagnostic would design targeted offers to replace it and test the exit on a ZIP-level split before the board commits to a full-year plan.

The read

The price increase paid for itself; the always-on discount does not. The +12% list price added about $2.5m of contribution for about 5.5% of same-market volume. At a 30% margin, 15% off with free removal needs 2.24 times the volume to stand still and has delivered about 1.06 times. Targeted offers cost a fraction as much, and a ten-week ZIP-level test would size the exit safely.

Net ticket moved through three regimes in one year: $5,263, then $5,883 after the increase, then $5,045 under the promotion

Each regime lasted four months. The increase held almost entirely at the point of sale; the promotion then took net ticket below where it was before the increase.

Implied elasticity is about −0.45 overall. It is highest on garage floors, the most quoted and most comparable surface, and close to zero on pool decks. Price became the leading lost reason, and the close rate fell in the quote band where garage jobs moved.

Caution

Implied elasticity divides the volume change by the price change and does not separate price from the funnel and lead-cost changes under way at the same time. The diagnostic would estimate it from quote-level close rates by price band and ZIP.

At a 30% margin, 15% off with free removal needs 2.24 times the volume to stand still; it has delivered about 1.06 times

A discount d at margin m leaves m − d(1 − 8%) per job of the original price, so volume must rise by m divided by that. Management's own figure, that volume must double, is the case with commission paid on list. The grids show how quickly the requirement rises as margin falls.

Note

Introducing an offer in May was a reasonable response to the volume decline that followed the January increase, with the peak season approaching. What four months of data now show is the scale: about $0.5m of contribution a month for about $25k returned.

Shark advertises below the local garage range and sells above it, and reps add discretionary discounts on top of the promotion

The website's "from" prices are the first price a customer sees; the in-home quote is often nearly twice that. Separately, reps who discount most often close least often, which suggests discretionary discounts are not buying the close.

Targeted offers cost a fraction of the always-on discount, and a ten-week ZIP-level test would size the exit with room to spare

Each alternative puts the offer where it changes a decision: a financed quote, a trough month, a failed coating, a second surface or an open quote. The exit test is designed to measure how much volume the business would give up, since the economics show the exit pays unless volume falls by more than half.

At this year's margin the always-on offer needs more than two and a half times the volume; targeted designs need a fraction of that, and a permanent price cut does not pay at the observed elasticity

Each control re-computes the exhibit from the break-even arithmetic on this tab. In the diagnostic the margin, removal cost and elasticity would be read from Shark's own quotes and jobs by market and surface.

Section 08 · Website & search

Website traffic is up about half on last year, but 3.6% of sessions request a quote; mobile speed, an 11-field form and Meta traffic landing on the homepage are the three fixable losses

Public search data shows a site that is found mostly by people who already know the name: 65% of organic visits are branded and 76% land on the homepage. The illustrative GA4 view shows where visitors are lost once they arrive. Together they point to a website lever worth $0.3m to $0.6m of annual contribution, most of it inside 90 days and none of it dependent on more spend.

The read

The website converts demand Shark already created and misses demand it could capture. Mobile carries 71% of sessions at little more than half desktop conversion, the 11-field form loses half its starters, and Meta traffic lands on the homepage at 1.8%. In public search data, organic is 65% branded and Shark buys none of the generic terms rivals buy. Five changes are worth $0.3m–0.6m a year; two can be live within six weeks.

Of 40,200 monthly sessions, 2,440 become a quote request or a call; most of the loss happens before a visitor reaches the form

Three in five sessions leave without engaging, and the quote form keeps fewer than half of those who start it. Meta visitors, a third of all traffic, convert at half the site average.

Section 09 · Sales & operations

Leads now wait 22 minutes for a first call and 4.6 days for a visit, and fewer close at the visit; restoring last year's rates is worth 300–450 installed jobs, and crews at 83% utilisation can absorb them

The sales process has not changed: the call centre takes the call and completes the Builder Prime form, a rep measures and quotes in the home, and crews install about ten days later. What changed is load. Leads rose 11% on the same call-centre team, and each step now takes longer and converts slightly worse. The diagnostic would confirm each delay from timestamps before any staffing or process change.

The read

The process is unchanged; every hand-off in it is slower. The median first call takes 22 minutes, up from 14, visits happen later, show rates fall with each day of delay, and same-visit closes dropped from 34% to 27%. Crews are not the constraint at company level. Restoring last year's funnel rates would add 300–450 installed jobs with no extra marketing.

The process is the same as last year; every hand-off in it is slower, and lead-to-installed has fallen from 20.9% to 18.9%

Seven stages, four owners and four systems sit between an inquiry and an installed floor. The front three stages, owned by the call centre and the in-home reps, account for nearly all of the conversion lost.

Section 10 · Competitive field

Shark meets 24 rival presences across its five markets and trails the national systems on 8 of 10 public scores; its edge is regional density and review volume

This tab is built on public data except where marked: competitor directories, Semrush exports of 16–17 July 2026, BBB and Birdeye profiles, company websites, transaction announcements and the July 2026 public diligence deck. Market context is kept in its own section and labelled external; none of it feeds a company figure elsewhere in the packet. The diagnostic would add what public data cannot see: competing quotes, win rates and price by ZIP.

The read

Shark competes in three tiers: four national franchise systems that each list 87 to 195 units, two PE-backed platforms assembled through 2026 transactions, and regional specialists that compete on price and local reviews. Public directories show 24 rival presences in Shark's five markets, nine of them in Central Florida. The July public matrix scores Shark below every national system on 8 of 10 factors, widest on adjacencies, trust and digital funnel. Its strengths are review volume and entry prices below the local garage band. Every published series puts category growth near 5% a year, so Shark's growth has to come from share and conversion.

Three tiers compete for the same Florida homeowner, and Shark sits between them: larger than the local specialists, a fraction of the national systems' footprint

National franchise systems bring brand, search budgets and storage bundles; the PE-backed platforms bring acquisition capital; local specialists bring price and neighbourhood reviews. Shark now has a sponsor of its own.

Section 11 · Tech & data stack

The systems are sound; the joins between them are not, so today only 38% of installed jobs can be traced from first touch to cash

Shark runs a stack typical of a multi-hub installer of its size: Builder Prime, GA4, Meta and Google ad accounts, QuickBooks, GreenSky and Birdeye. Each works for the team that uses it. Twelve of eighteen data flows between them are manual or missing, which is why marketing is read on leads rather than jobs and why Builder Prime and the ledger differ by $0.80m. None of the fourteen fixes replaces a system, and twelve fit inside the three-week window.

The read

Keep the systems, fix the joins. Four of eleven layers need only configuration (KEEP), five need a specific repair (FIX) and two are missing: call tracking and a reconciled reporting layer (ADD). The stack scores 2.4 of 5, and only 38% of installed jobs trace from first touch to cash, so channel, market and offer decisions rest on lead counts. Twelve fixes inside the diagnostic window would lift that to about 82% for new leads; moving the crew schedule into Builder Prime takes it past 90% within 90 days. About 50 days of effort in total, none of it a system replacement.

Eleven layers run the commercial engine: four should be kept as they are, five need a specific repair and two are missing

The verdicts are about fitness to measure the business at job level, not about how well each team uses its tool. Builder Prime, the ledger, GreenSky and Birdeye are assets; the gaps sit in calls, crews, the ad-platform feedback loop and reporting.

Section 12 · Cases & stress

Next year's contribution ranges from $6.6m to $11.7m, and the date the always-on offer ends explains more of that range than any storm, season or cost line

Three operating cases for September 2026 to August 2027, each with explicit drivers and monthly paths; a calendar of dated events, public and internal, with what each costs if it lands badly; and a floor that shows what the two mature hubs earn on their own. All company figures are illustrative and would be rebuilt on actual data in week one.

The read

The base case earns $10.3m of contribution in the next twelve months, 9% above last year, and it counts only decisions management controls, timed after a test or a gate. The downside, $6.6m, is the dated calendar landing against the business: the offer kept through the spring peak, higher Meta prices, a storm in October and a wet summer. The upside, $11.7m, decides the offer at week three. Weather is real but small, under $0.25m per event. Jacksonville and Central Florida cover the whole fixed-cost base 1.5 times today and 1.1 times in the downside.

Twelve-month contribution runs from $6.6m to $11.7m; the base case, $10.3m, is above last year without counting anything that has not been tested

Each case is a full set of operating drivers, not a percentage flex. The downside is the dated calendar resolving against the business with no credit for management response; the upside is every lever pulled early. September 2026 is the jump-off month and is the same in all three.

In the base case the offer accounts for 76% of the gain over the no-decision path; the operating levers add the rest from January

The base path is built month by month. Against a no-decision path, which leaves the always-on offer in place and earns $6.7m, replacing the offer after the ZIP test adds $2.7m; funnel, spend, Tampa and new-market pacing add $0.86m between them inside the twelve months.

The base counts $3.6m of the $4.8m–7.9m annual value at stake inside the year; nothing in it depends on an untested lift, a new hub or good weather

The discipline is the same as in an investment case: the base counts only decisions management controls and timings it could meet, the upside holds what needs evidence first, and some things are left out of every case so that none of them is quietly relied on.

The downside has dates on it: the offer decision in October, gate reviews in December and January, crew hiring before March, and two hurricane seasons

Conventional stress flexes volume by a percentage. Here the exposure is a calendar: some dates are public and fixed (the hurricane season, the wet season, two competitor transactions), others are decisions Shark or Vesterra will take on known dates. Each row carries its evidence label.

Landing alone, the offer left on all year costs $2.7m; every weather event costs less than $0.25m, and the largest external risk is lead volume

Each dated event is applied on its own to the base case, then the downside case is built by letting the adverse ones land together. Storms and rain matter, but they defer more than they destroy; the decisions on the calendar move more contribution than the weather does.

Caution

Storm and rain effects assume installs are deferred rather than lost and exclude property damage, insurance and any post-storm shift in household spending. The diagnostic would calibrate them on the 2024 and 2025 storm weeks in the crew schedule.

Jacksonville and Central Florida alone earn $8.7m of contribution, 1.53 times the company's whole fixed-cost base; in the downside they still cover it 1.14 times

The floor asks what the business earns if every growth assumption fails: Tampa and the new markets earn nothing, and only the two mature hubs carry the company. It is the number that bounds how wrong the cases can be. Hub fixed costs and overhead are illustrative (A-16) and are the first thing week one would replace.

Note

The floor is a strength of the business, not a forecast. Two hubs that cover the whole cost base with room to spare are what make it reasonable to take measured risk in Tampa and the new markets.

Three interactive reads let the board choose a case, land a dated event on it, and change the date of the offer decision

The escalation rules decide who hears about a drift, how fast and with what attached. They are written before the data is read, so the response to a red is a pre-agreed step rather than a meeting to decide what to do.

Caution

This is a back-cast on illustrative data, and the thresholds are the tab 14 targets for days 60 and 90, so several series sit outside them by design while the promotion runs. The diagnostic would set red limits on reconciled data before the first live Monday.

Note

Red is a request for a diagnosis, not a judgement on performance. Because every response is agreed in advance with its owner, the Monday board starts a conversation rather than a search for data.

Margin, first-call speed and Tampa sat outside their bands all summer; Meta frequency crossed its red limit in the fourth week and stayed there

Each series chart shows the weekly reading against its amber zone, the band between threshold and red limit. A reading inside the band is amber; beyond it on the wrong side, red.

Weekly feeds would have flagged each drift an average of 5.8 weeks before the monthly pack; call tracking and Builder Prime, both already in place, supply just over half of it

Lead time is measured on a back-cast over the trailing year: the week the weekly series first left its band, against the monthly management pack in which the same move would first have been visible. Feed provenance shows where each number comes from and how fresh it is on Monday morning.

Three interactive reads: the board for any market, any series against its band, and how fast a shock would trip each state

Each control re-draws the exhibit from the same illustrative base. In Dynamic Diagnostics the same views run on Shark's own feeds each Monday.

This tab sets out what the diagnostic would do day by day, what the board would receive at the end of week three, and what it asks of management: about twelve hours a week across five people. Every value on this tab is a range to be validated rather than a forecast, and the first week exists to replace illustrative figures with reconciled ones.

The read

Fifteen working days from read-only access to a board readout. Week one reconciles leads to jobs to revenue to bank; week two runs six workstreams on actual records; week three turns findings into decisions, test designs and a weekly monitor set. Management time is about twelve hours a week across five people. The offer decision memo is designed to be ready by day 15.

By day 15 the board would hold a reconciled baseline, a ranked value register and a weekly monitor set, all built on Shark's own records

Six levers are worth $4.8m to $7.9m of annual contribution, and the offer decision is half of it

Each lever is sized as an annual range of variable contribution before implementation cost. The diagnostic's job is to narrow each range, net out overlaps between levers and name an owner, before anything enters a plan.

Week one connects and reconciles, week two diagnoses in six workstreams, week three turns findings into decisions

The sequence is deliberate. No workstream reads a number until leads, jobs, revenue and cash reconcile, and the promotion memo is drafted early because it is the decision with the most contribution attached.

The board could take its first decision at the end of week one and the promotion decision by day 15

After day 15, more than twenty weekly monitors would tell the board within a week whether each decision is holding

Section 15 · Assumptions and method

Every number in this demo traces to a stated assumption or a public source

Company figures are illustrative and are labelled as such on every exhibit. They follow the structure of Shark's own systems so that, in week one of the diagnostic, each is replaced by the actual figure without changing the exhibit. Public figures are cited to their source and date.

Twenty assumptions carry the demo; three of them move the headline materially

Discount depth (A-14), the contribution definition (A-03) and the treatment of lead source (A-09) matter most. Click a column header to sort.

What the demo does, what the diagnostic adds, and what neither does

The demo shows the shape of the answer. The diagnostic produces the answer, on Shark's records, reconciled to the bank.

Method · this demo

Company figures are a calibrated illustration built to Builder Prime, GA4, ad-platform and ledger structures. Public figures come from Semrush exports of 16–17 July 2026, the company website, BBB and Birdeye profiles in September 2026, and Qualified Remodeler's 2024 profile.

Method · the diagnostic

Raw exports and read-only API access are reconciled from lead to installed job to revenue to bank deposit. Contribution is computed per job, and every exhibit in this demo is re-cut on those records.

Source · public anchors

2023 revenue $21.3m on 4,078 jobs (Qualified Remodeler). Acquisition by Vesterra Capital Partners announced 28 August 2026 (Angle Advisors). Published starting prices from the company website, September 2026.

What neither does

Neither sets prices, budgets or targets for management. Both state what the evidence supports, how strongly, and what it would cost to be wrong.

Scope

Scope

It is a demonstration of what a three-week diagnostic would produce for Shark, built on illustrative company data and real public data.

It is not an audit, a valuation or a critique of past decisions. Each tab poses a question management has raised, shows how the evidence would answer it, and names the test that settles it on Shark's own records (Exhibit 3.19). The structure, exhibit numbers and monitors carry over directly into the engagement.

Public figures are real; company figures are illustrative.

Semrush data (A-17), BBB and Birdeye profiles, published prices and the 2023 revenue anchor are public and cited. Revenue, jobs, marketing, funnel and hub figures are a calibrated model (A-02) built to match the context management has shared, such as VCM near 30%, Tampa near 10% and flat volume. Every exhibit's basis line says which applies.

The twelve months to August 2026, against the twelve months to August 2025.

Trailing periods (A-01) keep the price increase of January 2026 and the promotion of May 2026 inside one comparable year. Tab 03 also splits the year into three four-month regimes because the business changed twice within it (Exhibit 3.07).

Actual records, reconciled to cash, at job level.

The demo cannot see individual jobs, ZIPs, reps or ad sets. The diagnostic joins them, which is what allows incremental cost per job by channel (tab 04), elasticity by market and surface (tab 07) and contribution by drive-time band (tab 06) to be measured rather than modelled.

Reading the numbers

Interpretation

Revenue less install cost, commission, financing fees, warranty reserve and marketing.

It is before hub fixed costs and corporate overhead (A-03, A-16), which is why a hub can show positive VCM and still not cover its lease and manager. The definition matches the roughly 30% figure management uses; the diagnostic would confirm the classification line by line against the ledger.

Because contribution fell 8% while jobs were flat; the margin loss is larger and faster to reverse.

Price added about seven points of margin and the promotion with free removal took back about six (Exhibit 3.04). Volume matters too: established markets lost 7.3% of jobs (Exhibit 3.10), and new markets filled the gap at low margin. Fixing margin first protects cash while the volume work takes effect.

Because at 30% VCM, a 15-point price cut removes about half of each job's contribution.

With commission scaling with price, margin falls from 30% to about 16%, so volume must rise 1.85 times; free removal takes it to 2.24 times; management's own figure of 2.0 times assumes commission on list (tab 07). Observed lift was about 6% (Exhibit 3.07).

Each system counts something different, and none counts installed jobs caused by Meta.

Ads Manager counts view-through leads, Builder Prime counts the source the call centre records, and GA4 counts last-click form submits (tab 05). The diagnostic would join all three to the installed job and test incrementality with geographic holdouts.

The motion shows order and magnitude; the final frame is the exhibit.

Hover over any mark for the exact figure. Tables sort when a column header is clicked.

Data and access

Provenance

Read-only exports or API access to eight systems, listed in tab 14.

Builder Prime, GA4, Meta Ads Manager, Google Ads and Local Services Ads, call tracking, the general ledger, GreenSky and the crew schedule. Most of it exists today; call tracking and the link between GA4 and installed jobs are the only set-up work (tab 14).

About twelve hours a week across five people, most of it in week one.

The CEO's time is concentrated in the week-three readout; marketing and finance carry the data questions in week one (tab 14). No field or sales time is needed beyond short interviews.

Read-only, siloed per client, encrypted, and never used to train models.

The data-handling line on tab 02 sets out the controls. No model generates a figure; models suggest mappings and analysts approve them.

The ranking of levers would change little; the size of each would.

The promotion lever depends on A-14 and the observed lift. If the true lift were three times the demo's figure, the promotion would still return well under half of what it costs (tab 07). Value ranges (A-20) are deliberately wide and are not additive.

Findings

Findings

Probably by $0.75m to $1.1m, concentrated in pools least likely to be incremental.

Aggregator leads that rarely install, Meta frequency above about $35k a week, spend landing more than an hour from a hub, and new-market budgets set ahead of the hubs' ability to convert (tab 04). The diagnostic would measure, not infer, which of these dollars are incremental.

The demo pattern is consistent with that; the current data cannot prove it either way.

Branded search rises a week after Meta spend, Meta-sourced buyers more often hold competing quotes, and rivals buy the generic search terms Shark does not (tab 05). A geographic holdout would settle whether Meta is under- or over-credited.

On the demo economics, yes, but the test could not separate TV from season.

Cost per incremental job of about $2,050 sits just inside the $2,260 break-even and well above the blended $818 (tab 04). A cleaner read would use more markets and a pre-period (tab 05).

Distance, more than demand: jobs within 30 minutes of the hub earn about 21%, those beyond about 3%.

Drive time, callbacks and cancellations all rise with distance, and close rates are lower against dense franchise competition (tab 06). A tighter radius with inward backfill is worth $0.4m to $0.6m a year in the demo.

Partly; it cost about 5.5% of same-market volume and added about $2.5m of contribution.

On those figures the increase paid for itself. The loss of volume concentrated in garage jobs, where comparison shopping is heaviest (tab 07). The diagnostic would measure elasticity by market and surface rather than at company level.

Five changes worth $0.3m to $0.6m, led by the mobile form and Meta landing pages.

Mobile carries 71% of sessions at little more than half desktop conversion, the 11-field form loses half its starters, and Meta traffic lands on the homepage (tab 08). Organic search is largely branded, and Shark is absent from the paid and local-pack results where generic demand is captured.

Next steps

Process

A reconciled baseline, a ranked value register with evidence grades, decision memos and a set of weekly monitors.

The promotion decision memo and the marketing reallocation plan are the two items designed for an immediate board decision (tab 14). Test designs come with the sample and duration needed to read them.

The same evidence stays live as weekly monitors, each with a threshold and a named owner.

Dynamic Diagnostics reads the same source systems every week and writes a diagnosis for any breach, so the board sees drift in weeks rather than at the quarterly review (tab 02, tab 14).

The CreditSwan team listed on tab 02.

A short scoping call confirms system access and the week-one data request; the diagnostic can begin as soon as read-only access is in place.
